newsitem.title: USA: Senate rejects exception for budget balance.
newsitem.headline: Senate rejects exception for budget balance.

text.p: The Republican-led Senate Monday rejected a Democratic plan to permit the government to run a deficit when the economy turns sour as a way to protect the country from sliding into depression.

The change to the proposed balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution was defeated 64-35. The outlook is uncertain for the Senate vote later this month on the constitutional amendment, which would require the government to balance its books each year during peacetime.

Freshman Democratic Sen. Richard Durbin of Illinois sought to add the exception for an economic downturn or natural disaster, arguing the strict balanced budget requirement sought by Republicans was too restrictive.

More controversy surrounds wholesale changes Democrats will offer as the debate continues this month. The most controversial would exempt Social Security Trust Funds from the balanced budget ledgers, as requested by President Clinton.

The final vote on the constitutional amendment will be extremely close in both the House and Senate. If it passes by a two-thirds vote later this month in both houses, it must be ratified by 38 of 50 state legislatures, a process that could take seven years.

Durbin's change would have allowed a simple majority to approve deficit spending, not the "super majority" three-fifths vote required under the Republicans' budget amendment. The constitutional balanced budget amendment would also require a three-fifths vote to borrow money and would make it harder to raise taxes.
"Let's not be in a situation where we handcuff the American economy ... That just makes common sense," said Sen. Kent Conrad, Democrat of North Dakota.

Supporting their cause were more than 1,000 economists who said it could prevent the government from using economic stabilisers -- unemployment payments, federal spending and tax cuts -- to keep recessions from moving into depressions.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch replied that Congress would act if necessary. "If we have a true economic emergency we will get the three-fifths vote. If it isn't, if it doesn't measure up, the three-fifths vote won't be granted," the Utah Republican said.

In the House, the Judiciary Committee for the second time called off its vote on the amendment. Democrats said it was because Republicans were divided on whether Social Security Trust Funds should be used to balance the budget.

The Social Security issue poses the biggest threat to passage of the constitutional amendment. Republicans now have all 55 of their members and seven Democrats on board, and they are within one or two of reaching the magic 67 votes for passage.

In the House, the final vote had been originally scheduled for Feb. 26, but the Judiciary panel's delay could force a Senate vote first -- a boost for the cause among wavering House lawmakers if it passes.
In 1995, the amendment passed the House but went down by one vote in the Senate. Election-year changes in 1996 gave it more support in the Senate and cost it votes in the House.

President Clinton and several Democrats have pressed to take Social Security funds out of the budget, on the argument that including them makes it difficult to keep the fund solvent in the next century when the baby-boom generation retires.
